authoredSolutions.69: The implication is false only if \(p\land(\sim q)\) is true and \(p\Rightarrow(\sim q)\) is false. But \(p\land(\sim q)\) true forces \(p=T,\ q=F\), and then \(p\Rightarrow(\sim q)=\sim p\vee\sim q=T\). So the statement is never false — it is a tautology.
authoredSolutions.151: Since \(p\to q\equiv\sim p\vee q\), take \(\Delta=\vee\) and \(\nabla=\vee\): \((\sim p\vee q)\vee(p\vee q)=(p\vee\sim p)\vee q\equiv T\), a tautology. None of the other three combinations is a tautology, so \(\Delta=\vee,\ \nabla=\vee\).
authoredSolutions.178: Choosing 5 fruits with at least 2 oranges, at least one red apple and at least one white apple gives three cases for the counts \((R,W,O)\): \((1,1,3),(2,1,2),(1,2,2)\). Total \(={}^{7}C_{1}\,{}^{5}C_{1}\,{}^{8}C_{3}+{}^{7}C_{2}\,{}^{5}C_{1}\,{}^{8}C_{2}+{}^{7}C_{1}\,{}^{5}C_{2}\,{}^{8}C_{2}=1960+2940+1960=6860\).
